text: Eugene Schuyler (February 26, 1840 – July 16, 1890) was a nineteenth-century American scholar, writer, explorer, and diplomat. He was one of the first three Americans to earn a Ph.D. from an American university and the first American translator of Ivan Turgenev and Leo Tolstoy. He was the first American diplomat to visit Russian Central Asia and, as American Consul General in Istanbul, played a key role in publicizing Turkish atrocities in Bulgaria during the April Uprising of 1876. Schuyler was the first American Minister to Romania and Serbia, and U.S. Minister to Greece. Born in Ithaca, New York, on February 26, 1840, he was the son of Matilda (née Scribner) Schuyler and George W. Schuyler, a drugstore owner who later served as New York State Treasurer and member of the New York State Assembly. His sibling Walter S. Schuyler was a U.S. Army brigadier general, and his sister Martha was the mother of Major General Walter S. Grant. His father’s Dutch ancestors included Philip Schuyler, a general in George Washington’s army and a U.S. Senator, and his mother was the half-sister of Charles Scribner, founder of the Scribner publishing house. At fifteen, Schuyler entered Yale College, where he studied languages, literature, and philosophy; he graduated with honors in 1859 and was a member of Skull and Bones. In 1861, he earned a PhD in psychology and philosophy from Yale, becoming one of the first Americans to do so, alongside Arthur Williams Wright and James Morris Whiton; his dissertation, possibly titled "Wedgwood on English Philology," was later published in Bibliotheca Sacra in 1862. In 1860, he worked as an assistant to Noah Porter on the revision of Webster’s Dictionary, the first dictionary of American English. In 1862, he began studying law at Yale Law School and received his law degree from Columbia Law School in 1863. He practiced law in New York but found it uninteresting and instead began writing for The Nation, a role he maintained until his death. In September 1863, a Russian naval squadron stayed in New York harbor, and Schuyler met officers of the Russian flagship Alexander Nevsky, which inspired him to study Russian. He learned Russian well enough to translate Turgenev’s novel Fathers and Sons, published in the United States in 1867, the first such translation. That same year, he studied Finnish and completed the first American translation of the Finnish national epic, Kalevala, begun by John Addison Porter, who died in 1866. In 1864, Schuyler applied for a diplomatic post in the State Department, which took three years to consider; he was then appointed consul in Moscow, Russia’s second city. En route, he stopped in Baden-Baden to meet Turgenev, who gave him a letter of introduction to Leo Tolstoy. Schuyler began his diplomatic tour in Moscow in August 1867. In spring 1868, he traveled to the edge of Central Asia with a Russian merchant, Vasilii Alekseich, by steamboat down the Volga to Samara, then by carriage to Orenburg, where Russian forces were advancing toward Samarkand after occupying the Khanate of Bukhara in 1866. In 1868, he visited Tolstoy at Yasnaya Polyana, where Tolstoy was finishing War and Peace; Schuyler helped rearrange Tolstoy’s library and went hunting with him. Tolstoy, interested in public education in the United States, asked Schuyler for American primers and school textbooks, and Schuyler received permission to translate Tolstoy’s novel The Cossacks into English. In 1869, President Ulysses S. Grant’s administration removed Schuyler from Moscow and replaced him with a political appointee. He obtained a post as consul in Reval (now Tallinn). On November 1869, President Grant appointed Andrew Curtin, a former Pennsylvania Governor unfamiliar with Russia, as the new Minister to Russia; Curtin was impressed by Schuyler and appointed him secretary of the American legation in St. Petersburg, a position he held until 1876. Schuyler combined his diplomatic duties with scholarship and travel, beginning a major biography of Peter the Great and attending Russian Geographic Society meetings in St. Petersburg. In 1873, he was one of the first foreigners invited to visit Russia’s new Central Asian conquests. He left St. Petersburg on March 23, 1873, traveling first to Saratov, then by sledge to Orenburg, Kazala (now Kazalinsk), Fort Perovskii (now Kzyl-Orda), and later to Khiva, Turkistan, Shymkent, Tashkent, Samarkand, Bukhara, and Kokand, returning via Siberia and the Urals after eight months—though he had told the State Department he would be gone only three months—bringing back extensive geographical information. He wrote extensively about his journey for the National Geographic Society and submitted a detailed report to the State Department. He was embarrassed when his confidential report, critical of Russian General Konstantin Petrovich Von Kaufman’s treatment of the Tatars, was published in December 1876 in Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States – 1874 and translated into Russian by the St. Petersburg press. Despite this, Schuyler was generally favorable toward Russian presence in Central Asia, stating, “On the whole, the Russian influence is beneficial in Central Asia,” and that “it would be manifestly unjust to them to withdraw her protection and leave them to anarchy and to the unbridled rule of fanatical despots.” His two-volume book, Turkestan, was published in October 1876 in the United States and England and echoed his favorable view of Russian rule. Schuyler left Russia in 1876. He unsuccessfully sought the position of Minister to Turkey, which went to a political appointee of the Grant administration, and was instead given the role of secretary of the legation and consul general. He arrived in Istanbul on July 6, 1876, two months after the April Uprising in Bulgaria, which had been violently suppressed by the Ottoman Army. Schuyler learned of the massacres from Bulgarian students and faculty at Robert College in Constantinople. Vague reports first appeared in the British press on May 6, and American faculty at Robert College sent information to the British Minister to Turkey with no result, then to The Times and the London Daily News, which published its account on June 23, 1876. This caused a sensation in London, leading to a parliamentary discussion and a demand for an investigation by the opposition Liberal Party. The Conservative government of Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli agreed to investigate. The British appointed Walter Baring as second secretary to conduct the inquiry. Fearing a cover-up, Robert College faculty asked American Minister to Turkey Horace Maynard to conduct his own investigation, which he assigned to Schuyler. Schuyler prepared to travel to Bulgaria to investigate. By chance, his Russian friend Januarius MacGahan arrived in Constantinople to cover the Serbia-Turkish War, and Schuyler invited him to accompany him. They were joined by German journalist Karl Schneider (1854–1945), Georgian prince Aleksi Tsereteli (Aleksei Tseretelev), and Turkish and Bulgarian translator Petar Dimitrov, instructor at Robert College. They spent three weeks documenting atrocities in southern Bulgaria three months earlier. Schuyler reported to U.S. Minister to Turkey Horace Maynard that it was difficult to estimate the number of Bulgarians killed, but he estimated 15,000 for the districts he visited. He provided a vivid account of the village of Batak, stating that human bones, skulls, ribs, and complete skeletons were scattered everywhere, including a house with ashes and charred bones from thirty people burned alive, a pike where a village notable was roasted and buried, a foul hole with decomposing bodies, a mill dam filled with swollen corpses, a schoolhouse where 200 women and children were burned, and a churchyard with a thousand half-decayed forms, arms, feet, and heads protruding from stones. After his visit, the Mutessarif sent the Kaimakam of Tatar Bazardjik to Batak with lime to aid decomposition and prevent pestilence. Ahmed Aga, who commanded the massacre, was decorated and promoted to the rank of Yuz-bashi. Schuyler’s official report and MacGahan’s newspaper coverage caused a sensation in the British press. The Disraeli government tried to downplay the massacres, claiming Bulgarians were equally responsible, but Schuyler and MacGahan’s eyewitness accounts refuted this. When Russia threatened war against Turkey, Britain told the Turkish government it could not support Turkey due to public opinion. Russia, driven by Pan-Slavic sentiment and a desire to help Orthodox Christian Bulgarians, declared war on the Ottoman Empire in 1877 and invaded Bulgaria, leading to the Ottoman defeat and Bulgaria’s liberation in 1878. Schuyler’s role in Bulgaria’s liberation angered the Ottoman government, which protested to the U.S. government. Secretary of State Hamilton Fish was also displeased, as Schuyler acted without authorization. Fish considered withdrawing Schuyler but decided against it to avoid appearing unsympathetic to the Bulgarians. When President Rutherford B. Hayes took office, Schuyler faced further attacks in the press, accused of bias toward Bulgarians. On January 3, 1878, the Turkish government demanded his recall, stating that the Porte viewed his continued presence as a serious injury to Turkey’s diplomatic relations and administration. On May 29, 1878, a State Department investigation found that Schuyler’s sentiments were “strongly anti-Turkish” and that he “aided greatly to alienate British sympathy from Turkey,” reprimanding him for his “unauthorized and self-imposed mission to Bulgaria.” Schuyler was removed from Turkey and appointed consul in Birmingham, England, where he completed his translation of Tolstoy’s The Cossacks, published in 1878. In August 1879, he became consul general in Rome, where he finished his biography of Peter the Great and began a new book on Catherine the Great. A year later, he became Chargé d’affaires in Bucharest as the U.S. prepared to recognize Romania and Serbia’s independence. In Romania, he studied Romanian and became a corresponding member of the Romanian Academy of Sciences. On July 7, 1882, he was concurrently appointed Minister Resident/Consul General to Romania, Serbia, and Greece, residing in Athens. He presented his credentials to Romania on September 8, 1882, to Serbia on November 10, 1882, and to Greece on January 9, 1883. In July 1884, he was removed from the post when the U.S. Congress abolished the position of minister to Greece, Romania, and Serbia as an economy measure. He presented his recall on September 7, 1884, for Romania, transmitted by note by the Vice Consul General at Belgrade on September 19, 1884, for Serbia, and on October 13, 1884, for Greece. In 1884, Schuyler left the diplomatic service to lecture at Johns Hopkins and Cornell University on diplomatic practice and American diplomacy. His book American Diplomacy and the Furtherance of Commerce was published by Scribner’s in 1886, and according to his death notice in The New York Times, the publication “prevented him from becoming a member of the permanent staff of the State Department, where his experience would have made him especially useful.” In 1889, President Benjamin Harrison nominated him as First Assistant Secretary of State, but the nomination was withdrawn after opposition in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and William F. Wharton was appointed and confirmed. Instead, Schuyler became diplomatic agent and consul general in Cairo, Egypt, where he contracted malaria and died in Venice on July 16, 1890, at the age of fifty. He was buried in the Protestant section of the San Michele cemetery on the island of Isola di San Michele in Venice. On July 12, 1877, Schuyler married Gertrude Wallace "Gert" King (b. 1836) in Paris. She was the daughter of Charles King, former President of Columbia University, niece of former U.S. Representative and New York Governor John Alsop King, and granddaughter of both Rufus King and Nicholas Low. Her sister, Mary Alsop King Waddington, was a writer married to French Prime Minister William Henry Waddington. Mount Schuyler on Graham Land in Antarctica is named after Eugene Schuyler for his investigation of the Bulgarian April Uprising of 1876 and co-authoring the draft decisions of the 1876 Constantinople Conference. Streets in Sofia, Plovdiv, Varna, and Panagyurishte, Bulgaria, are named after him. Among the many curiosities Schuyler encountered in Russian Turkestan was the figure of the iskatchi, a person who sprinkles salt and bread over a corpse at a funeral and eats the bread later to cleanse the deceased of sins, sometimes for a fee, a practice common in Wales, Great Britain.

Among the various intriguing findings Schuyler made in Russian Turkestan is the figure of the iskatchi, which was common in Wales (Great Britain); this individual sprinkles salt and bread over a corpse at a funeral and then eats the bread later to cleanse the deceased man of his sins, sometimes charging a fee.
